texts.full_text: tified to see the broad discussion of our manuscript, "Use of SARS‐CoV‐2 infected deceased organ donors: Should we always 'just say no?'" and the companion manuscript by Shah et al, "Utilization of deceased donors during a pandemic: an argument against using SARS‐CoV‐2 positive donors."[^1^](#ajt16119-bib-0001){ref-type="ref"}, [^2^](#ajt16119-bib-0002){ref-type="ref"} Our viewpoint argues that the risk of SARS‐CoV‐2 transmission from asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic donors is likely very low. For selected patients with imminently life‐threatening organ failure, transplants from deceased donors with asymptomatic or mild SARS‐CoV‐2 infection may offer a favorable risk/benefit balance, although factors beyond transmission risk must also be considered. Recently, two case reports of non‐transmission from SARS‐CoV‐2 infected donors (1 platelet donor, 1 living liver donor) have been published which support our position. In "COVID‐19 transmission and blood transfusion: A case report," Cho et al[^3^](#ajt16119-bib-0003){ref-type="ref"} describe a patient with aplastic anemia treated with anti‐thymocyte globulin and cyclophosphamide who received a platelet transfusion from an asymptomatic SARS‐CoV‐2 infected donor. The recipient remained negative for SARS‐CoV‐2 by PCR testing 10 days post‐transfusion, despite having a robust immune response to other blood components. In "No evidence of transmission of SARS‐CoV‐2 from living liver donor to recipient," Saidi et al[^4^](#ajt16119-bib-0004){ref-type="ref"} report a case where a recipient of a living donor liver transplant remained negative for SARS‐CoV‐2 by PCR testing at day 7 post‐transplant, despite the donor being positive for SARS‐CoV‐2 on day 3 post‐transplant. texts.full_text: ct between them; and OCGA § 16-8-37 defined constructive possession as when one does not have actual custody but knows that a substance exists or its character and location. In this case before us the trial court ruled on motions to dismiss filed by Appellee, Alvarado. The central issue was whether there existed sufficient evidence for jury consideration regarding "actual" knowledge of cocaine in his possession under OCGA § 16-13-30(a)(2), which at that time defined trafficking as the sale or distribution with intent to distribute five grams (5) and more, but required proof beyond a reasonable doubt showing actual physical control over such quantity. Appellee argued for dismissal on grounds insufficient evidence was presented indicating he had "actual" possession of cocaine knowing it existed. The trial court granted this motion finding no direct testimony placing the drugs in Appellant's immediate presence nor sufficient circumstantial evidence connecting him directly to having knowledge and exerciseable dominion or control over a quantity exceeding five grams. We reverse that ruling, holding there was enough competent proof for submission at least as concerns constructive possession with knowing intent. Evidence showed Alvarado had been seen near the location where drugs were sold; he frequented this area often making transactions which included cocaine purchases by undercover officers posing buyers in those instances without his direct apprehension or confrontation. Furthermore other witnesses described seeing him acting suspiciously around times of drug sales, and surveillance cameras captured images placing Appellee within close proximity to suspected traffickers. While actual physical control may not have been conclusively established from this evidence alone it did support an inference he had both knowledge about the cocaine's presence as well its illegal nature coupled with exercising dominion over said substance in some manner
